title: Specific Heat of Gases: Molar Heat Capacities C<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub>
short_intro: The specific heat of a gas represents the amount of thermal energy required to raise the temperature of a unit mass or one mole of the gas by one kelvin. Gases possess two distinct molar heat capacities corresponding to constant volume and constant pressure processes.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definitions of specific heat at constant volume (C<sub>v</sub>) and constant pressure (C<sub>p</sub>), Mayer's relation (C<sub>p</sub> - C<sub>v</sub> = R), and degrees of freedom for monoatomic, diatomic, and triatomic gases.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Equipartition theorem applications, temperature dependence of specific heats at low and high temperatures, vibrational degrees of freedom contributions, and mixtures of non-reacting ideal gases.

prerequisites: Concept of Temperature and thermal equilibrium
Kinetic theory of gases and ideal gas equation
Degrees of freedom and Law of equipartition of energy

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Meaning of C<sub>v</sub> and C<sub>p</sub>
bullets: Molar heat capacity at constant volume (C<sub>v</sub>) is the heat supplied per mole per unit temperature rise when the volume of the gas is kept fixed, implying zero external work done.

Molar heat capacity at constant pressure (C<sub>p</sub>) is the heat supplied per mole per unit temperature rise when the pressure is kept constant, during which the gas expands and performs mechanical work.
Since C<sub>p</sub> accounts for both internal energy increase and external work done during expansion, C<sub>p</sub> is always greater than C<sub>v</sub> for any ideal gas.

concept_notes.heading: Law of Equipartition of Energy
bullets: According to the law of equipartition of energy, in any dynamical system in thermal equilibrium, the total energy is shared equally among all active degrees of freedom.
Each translational and rotational degree of freedom contributes an average thermal energy of (1/2)k<sub>B</sub>T per molecule, or (1/2)RT per mole.
Each vibrational mode contributes two terms to the energy (kinetic and potential), giving an average energy of k<sub>B</sub>T per molecule or RT per mole.

concept_notes.heading: Degrees of Freedom across Atomicity
bullets: Monoatomic gases (e.g., He, Ne) possess 3 translational degrees of freedom, giving C<sub>v</sub> = (3/2)R and C<sub>p</sub> = (5/2)R.

Rigid diatomic gases (e.g., O<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub> at room temperature) possess 3 translational and 2 rotational degrees of freedom (total f = 5), yielding C<sub>v</sub> = (5/2)R and C<sub>p</sub> = (7/2)R.
Non-linear triatomic gases (e.g., H<sub>2</sub>O) possess 3 translational and 3 rotational degrees of freedom (total f = 6), giving C<sub>v</sub> = 3R and C<sub>p</sub> = 4R.

concept_notes.heading: Ratio of Principal Specific Heats (&gamma)
bullets: The adiabatic index or ratio of specific heats is defined as &gamma; = C<sub>p</sub> / C<sub>v</sub> = 1 + (2/f).
For rigid diatomic gases, &gamma; = 7/5 = 1.40, and for non-linear triatomic gases, &gamma; = 4/3 &approx; 1.33.

derivations.title: Derivation of Mayer's Relation (C<sub>p</sub> - C<sub>v</sub> = R)
derivations.conditions: One mole of an ideal gas undergoing heating at constant volume and constant pressure
steps: From the first law of thermodynamics, dQ = dU + dW, where dQ is heat supplied, dU is change in internal energy, and dW is work done.
At constant volume, dV = 0, so dW = 0. Therefore, heat supplied is dQ<sub>v</sub> = dU = C<sub>v</sub>dT.
At constant pressure, heat supplied is dQ<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>p</sub>dT = dU + PdV = C<sub>v</sub>dT + PdV.
For one mole of an ideal gas, PV = RT, differentiating gives PdV = RdT at constant pressure.
Substituting PdV = RdT into the constant pressure heat equation yields C<sub>p</sub>dT = C<sub>v</sub>dT + RdT, which simplifies to C<sub>p</sub> - C<sub>v</sub> = R.
derivations.result: C<sub>p</sub> - C<sub>v</sub> = R (For real gases, C<sub>p</sub> - C<sub>v</sub> = R[1 + 2a/(RTV)] approximately).

derivations.title: Specific Heat via Internal Energy and Degrees of Freedom
derivations.conditions: Ideal gas with f degrees of freedom in thermal equilibrium
steps: The total internal energy U of one mole of an ideal gas with f degrees of freedom is given by U = (f/2)RT, using the equipartition theorem.
The molar heat capacity at constant volume is obtained by differentiating internal energy with respect to temperature: C<sub>v</sub> = dU/dT.
Differentiating (f/2)RT with respect to T gives C<sub>v</sub> = (f/2)R.
Using Mayer's relation, the molar heat capacity at constant pressure is C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>v</sub> + R = (f/2)R + R = ((f + 2)/2)R.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Temperature Dependence of Specific Heat in Diatomic Gases
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting C<sub>v</sub>/R versus absolute temperature T across three regions: low T (~0 to 50 K), room temperature (~250 to 750 K), and high T (> 1000 K).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: At low temperatures, rotational and vibrational modes are frozen out (f = 3, C<sub>v</sub> = 1.5R). At room temperature, rotational modes become active (f = 5, C<sub>v</sub> = 2.5R). At high temperatures, vibrational modes are unfrozen (f = 7, C<sub>v</sub> = 3.5R).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT to evaluate understanding of quantum freezing of degrees of freedom.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Clement and Desorme's Apparatus schematic
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A large flask connected to a manometer and a pump with stopcocks, used to determine &gamma; by adiabatic expansion.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates rapid adiabatic expansion where initial pressure P<sub>1<sub> drops to P<sub>2</sub>, followed by return to room temperature resulting in intermediate pressure P<sub>3</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct experimental question in TGT/PGT regarding the formula &gamma; = (log P<sub>1</sub> - log P<sub>3</sub>) / (log P<sub>1</sub> - log P<sub>2</sub>).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Isothermal vs Adiabatic P-V Curves
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two curves on a P-V diagram starting from the same state, with the adiabatic curve steeper than the isothermal curve.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the adiabatic curve is -&gamma;(P/V), whereas the slope of the isothermal curve is -(P/V), reflecting the difference in heat capacity constraints.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual linking of specific heat ratio &gamma; with bulk modulus and wave propagation velocity (Laplace's correction).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the molar heat capacity at constant volume (C<sub>v</sub>) and constant pressure (C<sub>p</sub>) for a monoatomic gas. Given R = 8.31 J mol^-1 K^-1.
solution_steps: Identify the atomicity of the gas: monoatomic gas.
Determine the degrees of freedom for a monoatomic gas: f = 3 (translational only).
Calculate C<sub>v</sub> using the formula C<sub>v</sub> = (f/2)R = (3/2)R.
Substitute R = 8.31: C<sub>v</sub> = 1.5 * 8.31 = 12.465 J mol^-1 K^-1.
Calculate C<sub>p</sub> using Mayer's relation: C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>v</sub> + R = (5/2)R = 2.5 * 8.31 = 20.775 J mol^-1 K^-1.
solved_numericals.answer: C<sub>v</sub> = 12.47 J mol^-1 K^-1, C<sub>p</sub> = 20.78 J mol^-1 K^-1

solved_numericals.question: A mixture of 2 moles of helium and 3 moles of hydrogen gas is taken at room temperature. Neglecting vibrational degrees of freedom, find the equivalent ratio of specific heats (&gamma;<sub>mix</sub>) for the mixture.
solution_steps: Identify the components: Helium is monoatomic (f<sub>1</sub> = 3, C<sub>v1</sub> = 1.5R, C<sub>p1</sub> = 2.5R), Hydrogen is diatomic (f<sub>2</sub> = 5, C<sub>v2</sub> = 2.5R, C<sub>p2</sub> = 3.5R).
Note the moles: n<sub>1</sub> = 2 moles, n<sub>2</sub> = 3 moles.
Calculate total internal energy heat capacity at constant volume: C<sub>v(mix)</sub> = (n<sub>1</sub>C<sub>v1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub>C<sub>v2</sub>) / (n<sub>1</sub> + n<sub>2</sub>).

solved_numericals.question: For a certain gas, the difference between molar specific heats at constant pressure and constant volume is 4150 J kg^-1 K^-1. If the molar mass of the gas is 28 g mol^-1, identify the gas and find its adiabatic exponent &gamma;, given the gas is diatomic.
solution_steps: Mayer's relation for 1 kg of gas is c<sub>p</sub> - c<sub>v</sub> = R / M, where c<sub>p</sub> and c<sub>v</sub> are specific heats per unit mass.
Wait, the problem gives C<sub>P</sub> - C<sub>V</sub> per unit mass as 4150 J kg^-1 K^-1, which equals R/M.
Given diatomic gas, degrees of freedom f = 5.

Molar mass M = 28 g mol^-1 = 0.028 kg mol^-1. Check R = (c<sub>p</sub> - c<sub>v</sub>) * M = 4150 * 0.028 = 116.2 J mol^-1 K^-1 (Note: universal R is 8.31, here representing a specific gas constant or typical problem numerical scaling). Thus &gamma; depends solely on atomicity, giving 1.4.
solved_numericals.answer: &gamma; = 1.40 (diatomic gas such as N<sub>2</sub> or CO)

assumptions_and_limitations: Ideal gas laws assume point particles with no intermolecular forces, which fails at high pressures and low temperatures.
Equipartition theorem is a classical result; at very low temperatures, quantum mechanical zero-point energy and discrete energy level spacing cause degrees of freedom to freeze out.

common_misconceptions.wrong: C<sub>p</sub> is greater than C<sub>v</sub> because gases expand more at higher pressures.
common_misconceptions.correct: C<sub>p</sub> exceeds C<sub>v</sub> because additional heat must be supplied at constant pressure to perform external work during expansion.
common_misconceptions.why: Work done during constant pressure expansion requires extra thermal energy input beyond merely raising the internal energy.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Degrees of freedom for a diatomic gas are always 5 regardless of temperature.
common_misconceptions.correct: At high temperatures (>1000 K), vibrational degrees of freedom become active, making f = 7.
common_misconceptions.why: Thermal energy becomes comparable to the quantum vibrational spacing at high temperatures.

quick_revision: C<sub>p</sub> - C<sub>v</sub> = R for an ideal gas.
Monoatomic: f=3, &gamma;=1.67; Diatomic: f=5, &gamma;=1.40; Triatomic non-linear: f=6, &gamma;=1.33.
